Get Smart: As the STI Dips, is it Time to Buy?
article:
We get plenty of questions at The Smart Investor.
But there’s one that comes up most often:
“What stock should I buy?”
Right now, it’s a question that’s likely on the minds of many investors.
As of last Friday, 23 October 2026, the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) was down 7% from its 52-week high.
It’s not quite a market correction — that would be a decline of 10% or more.
But after a bull run, the stock market is starting to get bargain hunters interested again.
Especially if you’ve got money set aside.
But here’s the thing: before you ask what to buy, there’s a more important question …
… what stock do you NEED?
You see, different investors have different needs.
And different stocks play different roles.
Ask a stock to do a job it wasn’t built for, and you’re setting yourself up for disappointment.
Picture a pyramid
At The Smart Investor, we like to view a dividend portfolio as a pyramid.
Take a moment to picture one in your head.
At the bottom, where it’s widest, you want a strong foundation.
These are your workhorses — companies or REITs that turn up every quarter or every six months to deliver steady, reliable dividends.
They don’t offer a lot of growth.
But they are reliable.
My colleague, David Kuo, calls them Income Stocks.
Only when you have that stable base do you start layering on growth.
These are your Growth Stocks.
The middle of the pyramid is a designated area for stocks that have the ability to grow their sales and profits — so that they can pay you higher dividends in the future.
Finally, at the very tip, the smallest part of the pyramid, is what I call your testing ground.
This is your speculative space, where you let yourself run a little.
Let me show you what I mean with two Singapore stocks.
The base: the REIT that turns up
First up,
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT.
The REIT owns popular malls and offices, mostly in Singapore.
It’s not flashy. It won’t make headlines.
So what makes it special?
CICT is one of a handful of REITs that have increased their distribution per unit (DPU) — the REIT version of a dividend per share — since 2021.
That may not sound spectacular.
Until you consider what has happened since.
We had the steepest interest rate hikes in decades.
We had Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs.
We had the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Through it all, CICT’s DPU has inched up every year since 2021 like clockwork.
That’s exactly what you want at the bottom of your pyramid: a REIT that turns up, pays you, and doesn’t need you to think about it.
Just don’t expect fireworks.
Expecting 20% growth out of CICT is a bridge too far.
The middle: simple, but not easy
One level up, we have supermarket operator
Sheng Siong
(SGX: OV8).
The best way to describe Sheng Siong’s business?
Simple, but not easy.
Everyone’s been to a Sheng Siong before.
The business is easy to understand.
But it’s really, really hard to do.
Its secret?
In my eyes, Sheng Siong does the simple things really, really well.
For starters, the supermarket operator keeps adding new stores — from 27 at its IPO in 2011 to 90 today.
And it uses money from its existing operations to fund the new store buildout, not debt.
At the same time, it has made its stores more profitable.
Fresh food and house brands play a big part here, made possible by its Mandai distribution centre, which allowed Sheng Siong to cut out the middleman and buy directly from the source.
In short: more stores, and better stores.
It sounds easy. It isn’t.
To be sure, there are risks to watch.
Sheng Siong is building a hefty new warehouse in Sungei Kadut, which could limit the cash available for dividends.
And with the Johor Bahru-Singapore RTS Link on the way, nobody knows how our grocery habits will change until the rubber hits the road.
That’s the trade-off in the middle of the pyramid: a little more uncertainty, in exchange for a business that can grow.
The tip: keep it small
Now for the fun part.
The tip is the most exciting part of the pyramid.
It’s where the big stories live, and it’s tempting to let it grow.
The base, on the other hand, can feel dull.
When a hot stock is flying, a REIT quietly paying its dividends won’t exactly get your pulse racing.
But think about what happens when the tip gets too big.
The whole pyramid becomes unbalanced.
That’s why the testing ground is a controlled area — and you want to be strict about it.
In practice, it comes down to how much you put into each stock.
Bigger positions for the workhorses at the base.
Smaller ones for the ideas at the tip.
That way, if a testing-ground idea doesn’t work out, it stings.
But your foundation holds.
Get Smart: Give every stock a job
So, as you draw up your shopping list during this dip, pause before asking “what stock should I buy?”
Ask what your portfolio needs instead.
If your base is shaky, you probably need a reliable workhorse, not the next big thing.
If your base is solid, you have room to add some growth.
And if you want to scratch that speculative itch, do it at the tip.
Again, keep it small.
Plainly speaking, before you give a stock your money, give it a job.
That’s how we think about dividend investing at The Smart Investor.
If you’d like to see that thinking in action, the Smart Dividend Portfolio is where we put it to work.

title: Adani Group said to seek US$1.5 bil for data centre financing  — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 3): Adani Group, controlled by India’s richest man Gautam Adani, is seeking to borrow about US$1.5 billion to help finance its expansion into data centres, according to people familiar with the matter.

AdaniConneX Pvt, a joint venture with data centre operator EdgeConneX, is in talks with lenders including DBS Group Holdings Ltd, First Abu Dhabi Bank PJSC and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc for the offshore facility, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information.

Adani Group plans to invest about US$100 billion in data centres and other digital infrastructure by 2035, building on its sprawling energy business. Billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance conglomerate also plans to plow as much as US$110 billion over seven years into artificial intelligence-related infrastructure.

The broader push is fueling a surge in India’s data centre market as conglomerates race to build the computing capacity required for AI and cloud services. The government expects capacity to surge to nearly eight gigawatts by 2030 from about 1.57 gigawatts in August 2026, while the country could draw roughly US$200 billion of investment into the sector over the next seven to eight years, local media reported.

The Adani conglomerate is also holding talks with other lenders including Natixis SA, ING Bank NV and Societe Generale SA for the latest financing, the people said. Discussions over pricing are taking place and the loan could have a tenor of five to seven years, they said. The terms haven’t been finalised.

DBS and FAB declined to comment while the Adani Group, MUFG, Societe Generale, Natixis, ING did not reply to emails seeking comment.

See also: TSMC’s US$265 bil campus driving real estate boom in Phoenix suburbs

Adani’s latest funding drive comes months after AdaniConneX secured an US$800 million data centre loan, which had an 18-month duration.

title: Asian stocks fall after US losses; oil holds drop
article:
(Nov 3): Asian stocks declined on Tuesday morning after a sell-off in US chipmakers deepened, overshadowing a plunge in oil prices amid optimism over diplomatic progress towards ending the war in Iran.

The MSCI Asia-Pacific gauge dropped 0.6% with South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi Index sliding more than 2%. The decline came after a gauge of US chipmakers extended a three-day rout to 12% and the Nasdaq 100 sank 10% from its peak, entering a technical correction. In a sign some investors are looking to buy the dip, US stock futures gained. Japanese markets were closed for a holiday.

Chinese equities opened lower even after the central bank said it will encourage financial institutions to make greater use of stock-support tools and optimise their terms as authorities seek to bolster market stability.

Apple Inc’s shares fell in late US trading after the company delivered a mixed outlook to investors in its first quarterly report under chief executive officer John Ternus, with narrower profit margins overshadowing an upbeat sales forecast. Elsewhere, Anthropic PBC disclosed a 12-fold increase in quarterly revenue while outlining plans to spend more than US$895 billion ($1.15 trillion) in the coming years.

Brent crude held losses from Monday when it slumped 7.6% to close at US$104.77 a barrel as traders assessed signs of progress towards ending the conflict, a day before Americans vote in the midterm elections.

See also: Stock sell-off eases in Asian trade as oil declines

Easing geopolitical tensions are lowering energy prices and inflation risks, yet the drop in crude has so far failed to revive appetite for technology shares as concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending and stretched valuations persist.

“Lower oil should be a tailwind for tech, but the fact that stocks could not hold the open even with crude plunging shows how little conviction is left even after last week’s carnage,” said Dave Mazza, the CEO of Roundhill Financial.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government had been granted more authority by the country’s supreme leader to pursue peace talks, while US President Donald Trump hinted at progress in negotiations.

See also: Stocks slump as Wall Street gets AI wake-up call

“They want to make a deal, and that could happen,” Trump told reporters in Washington. He added that oil prices had fallen because “it looks like that’s coming together very nicely” and “people found out about it”.

Moments later, Trump mouthed “no” when a reporter shouted a question about whether he would resume military strikes on Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections.

China’s CSI 300 Index dropped 0.5% at the open amid scepticism over the latest market support measures from the authorities. The two liquidity-injection tools — a swap facility and relending operations to encourage more stock purchases— reappeared with some adjustments as authorities sought to bolster market stability and confidence.

Chinese shares have been mired in a slump since the summer, weighed down by a weak economy and doubts over AI earnings. Previous attempts to revive the market — including a round of buying by the so-called national team starting July, and regulatory guidance to curb selling last month — have fallen short. The CSI 300 benchmark fell 8.5% in October in its worst month in more than a decade.

Elsewhere, a Bloomberg gauge of the dollar was little changed on Tuesday, while US Treasury 10-year futures slipped 5/32. There’s no trading of cash Treasuries in Asia due to the holiday in Japan.

Concerns over AI spending were also in focus as big technology companies returned to US bond markets to fund their investment plans. After an almost three-month borrowing drought, they are flooding back in.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Oracle Corp is selling US$10 billion of bonds alongside an equal amount of equity, while Meta Platforms Inc is eyeing at least US$20 billion from a potential sale in multiple currencies. Microsoft Corp sold US$25 billion of bonds last Thursday, its first US offering since 2017, while Alphabet Inc tapped Europe’s bond market on Monday for the second time this year.

The economic calendar adds another potential catalyst for the markets. US manufacturing activity picked up in October, supported by the strongest increase in production in nearly five years, while investors are looking ahead to a series of labour-market reports.

US job openings data due Tuesday are expected to show that listings edged higher in September, while weekly jobless claims on Thursday are seen remaining near historically low levels. Economists expect Friday’s payrolls report to show job growth more than doubled to 65,000 in October, with the unemployment rate holding at 4.2%.

“It’s going to be an extremely interesting week in the markets,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak. “We will have political issues to decipher as well as geopolitical ones. And growing doubts about AI investment returns will likely matter much more than historical patterns in determining the market’s direction going forward.”
• Palantir Technologies Inc gave a forecast for full-year revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations, buoyed by surging demand for the company’s data analytics tools.
• Marvell Technology Inc agreed to buy Lumentum Holdings Inc at an enterprise value of US$115 billion, clinching one of the largest technology deals in history in a push to capitalise on runaway data centre spending.
• Snap Inc has settled a lawsuit filed by two teenagers who say years of compulsive scrolling and posting on the company’s photo-sharing app contributed to their mental health struggles.

Some of the main moves in markets:
• S&P 500 futures were little changed as of 10.34am Tokyo time on Tuesday
• The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index was little changed
• The euro was little changed at US$1.1186
• The Japanese yen was little changed at 157.93 per dollar
• The offshore yuan fell 0.2% to 6.6633 per dollar

title: Disney plans thousands of layoffs, targeting 20% cost savings — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 3): Walt Disney Co is moving toward thousands of job cuts with the entertainment giant asking some managers to target 20% in annual cost savings, according to people familiar with the matter.

The savings could come from job eliminations, as well as from expense reductions, said the people, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private.

Some of Disney’s operations, which range from theme parks, TV network and the movie studio, will be affected disproportionately. Chief executive officer Josh D’Amaro aims to reinvest a portion of the savings into film and TV programming, technology and the theme parks and cruise ship businesses, the people said.

The company has promised double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share in the current fiscal year.

Disney has cut billions of dollars worth of costs and eliminated thousands of positions in recent years, with reductions impacting every division including ABC, Pixar, ESPN, the film studio and the experiences unit. The company had 231,000 people worldwide at the end of the last fiscal year.

See also: Euronext joins industry push to integrate Nordic capital markets

The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 1 that Disney was planning a restructuring of its TV division, and cuts at the company’s legal and global affairs unit.

Other entertainment companies including Netflix Inc, Sony Pictures Entertainment and Skydance Corp’s Paramount and Warner Bros divisions have also cut jobs as revenue from traditional television declines and streaming subscriber growth slows. The also have to cope with more viewers tuning to social media, online videos and streaming services backed by tech giants like Amazon.com Inc and Apple Inc.

At the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles last month, Disney president Dana Walden said that “there is a need to constantly evaluate how you’re structured and how big is the organisation. Technology set their sights on our business and we must survive and thrive and grow, and that’s what we’re going to do.”
